planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost danger passes, in a site with morning shade for the first two seasons.

directions: Mitchell originated as a wild selection found in Franklin County, Illinois, and was later included in Kentucky State University's regional pawpaw variety trials alongside Sunflower and KSU-Atwood. It sets fruit reliably on a vigorous, disease-resistant tree and benefits from cross-pollination with a genetically distinct cultivar planted nearby. Grow in deep, moist, well-drained soil and mulch heavily to keep the shallow root system cool. Hand-pollinate with a small paintbrush in home orchards if fruit set is sparse, since pawpaw flies attract few natural pollinators.

planting.note: Set out grafted stock in spring and stake young trees, which are prone to wind-whip until established.

directions: Middletown is one of the older named pawpaw selections, tracing to Middletown, Ohio, and documented in historic cultivar surveys compiled by Kentucky State University. It performs well as a dooryard tree in the Ohio Valley climate it originated in. Provide part shade while young, since pawpaw is naturally an understory species, then transition to more sun once the tree is fruiting-age. Feed lightly with a balanced organic fertilizer in early spring and keep the root zone consistently moist through fruit development.

planting.note: Plant in spring in a sheltered spot; this early-ripening selection benefits from a full-sun site once mature to speed fruit finish.

directions: Quaker Delight was selected at Wilmington College in Ohio and has placed well at the Ohio Pawpaw Festival tastings for its creamy texture and mild flavor. It ripens earlier than many named pawpaws, typically by early September, making it useful for extending the home harvest window when paired with later cultivars. Plant a second unrelated cultivar nearby for pollination, since pawpaw is self-incompatible. Mulch well and avoid waterlogged sites, as roots are sensitive to standing water.

planting.note: Transplant grafted trees in spring; this selection sets fruit reliably even after late frosts, so it tolerates less-sheltered sites than most pawpaws.

directions: Green River Belle was found growing wild near the Green River in Hart County, Kentucky, and selected in 1998 for its large fruit and subtle cinnamon-tinged flavor. It shows good resistance to Phyllosticta leaf spot, a common pawpaw fungal issue in humid climates, making it a lower-maintenance choice for home growers. Site it in rich, slightly acidic soil with reliable moisture and cross-pollinate with a genetically unrelated pawpaw. Protect young trees from rabbits and deer, which will browse the bark and foliage.
sources: Kentucky heirloom fruit tree grower records

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in early spring on well-drained sandy soils where it thrives even under nematode pressure.

directions: Tice originated in the Ft. Myers, Florida area and is prized as one of the most nematode-resistant mulberries available, making it a favored rootstock as well as a fruiting selection for sandy Gulf Coast soils. It produces large, sweet-tart, juicy berries on a vigorous, wide-canopied tree with notably large leaves and weeping outer branches. Give it full sun and irrigate during establishment; once rooted it is quite drought tolerant. Net or harvest promptly, as ripe fruit drops heavily and stains hardscape below.

planting.note: Plant in spring with room to spread; this heritage variety grows large and drops fruit over an extended season, so site it away from paving and patios.

directions: Hicks Everbearing is a heritage North Carolina selection long thought lost before being rediscovered and reintroduced by fruit collector A.J. Bullard. It is more cold-hardy than black mulberry and drops slender, dark, mildly flavored berries continuously for up to four months, historically valued as a hog-forage tree as much as a table fruit. Plant in full sun on rich, moist soil and expect a long-lived, large-statured tree; it can live over a century. Because fruiting continues so long, plan for a mulched drop zone or plant it well away from walkways.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; American persimmon has a long taproot, so choose the final site carefully to avoid transplant shock.

directions: Dollywood was introduced by Illinois breeder James Claypool and is grown for its remarkably large, exceptionally sweet fruit on a spreading, productive tree. Full astringency until fully soft-ripe is typical of American persimmon, so let fruit color deeply and soften on the tree before harvest. It tolerates poor and compacted soils once established and needs little supplemental water in most regions. Because most American persimmons are dioecious, plant a male pollinator nearby unless the cultivar is confirmed self-fertile.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society, 'Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars' (2025)

planting.note: Plant in spring in the coldest site on the property where persimmon is hardy; this selection was bred specifically for cool-climate reliability.

directions: Geneva Red was bred by George Slate at the Geneva, New York experiment station and is valued as one of the earliest-ripening, sweetest American persimmons suited to short, cool growing seasons. It sets fruit reliably even where summers are marginal for other native persimmon selections. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil and avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization, which promotes vegetative growth at the expense of fruit. Allow fruit to fully soften after coloring, as unripe flesh remains strongly astringent.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society, 'Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars' (2025)

planting.note: Plant in spring on a deep, well-drained site; this early-ripening cultivar rewards a sunny position with faster fruit finish.

directions: Osage is a 21st-century Oklahoma selection valued for heavy, reliable bearing of medium-sized, flavorful fruit that ripens earlier than many older American persimmon cultivars. Its early ripening makes it a good match for shorter-season regions or gardeners who want to beat the first hard freeze. Plant in full sun and resist the urge to over-irrigate mature trees, which are naturally drought tolerant thanks to a deep taproot. Thin heavy fruit sets in vigorous years to reduce limb breakage.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society, 'Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars' (2025)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun to develop the best red blush on the ripening fruit.

directions: Barbara's Blush, also sold under its breeding number WS8-10, was developed by Indiana breeder Jerry Lehman and named for his wife. The fruit develops an attractive pinkish-red blush that extends into the flesh and carries an intensely sweet, honey-like flavor with a smooth, melting texture. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil; this selection has shown good disease resistance in home orchard trials. As with all American persimmons, wait for full softening after color break before harvesting to avoid puckering astringency.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society, 'Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars' (2025)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall; its narrow columnar habit suits tight side yards and foundation plantings.

directions: Standing Ovation is a narrow, upright saskatoon selection marketed under the First Editions brand, forming a tidy column reaching about 15 feet tall on a 3-foot spread, making it an unusually space-efficient native fruiting shrub. Bronze new growth matures to green and turns brilliant orange, red, and purple in fall, alongside small, sweet, edible blue-black berries in early summer. Plant in full sun for the best fruit set and fall color, in average, well-drained soil. Prune lightly in late winter only to remove dead or crossing wood, since the naturally columnar form needs little shaping.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in lime-free, well-drained soil; site as a small specimen tree or large multi-stem shrub.

directions: Ballerina is a vase-shaped hybrid serviceberry that blooms and fruits about a week later than most cultivars, extending the harvest window for its sweet, blue-black berries. Bronze-red spring foliage matures to green, then turns orange and purple in autumn, giving strong three-season interest. It shows good resistance to fireblight, a common concern in the rose family, and adapts to a wide range of soils as long as drainage is decent. Grow in full sun to light shade and net the ripening fruit if birds are a problem, since they find it just as appealing as gardeners do.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized suckering shrubs in early spring; allow room for it to form a spreading thicket.

directions: Forestburg is a prairie-bred saskatoon cultivar developed for the harsh growing conditions of the northern Great Plains and Canadian prairies, ripening among the earlier-maturing cultivars in comparative trials. It produces good yields of sweet, almond-flavored, blueberry-like fruit prized for jams, pies, and fresh eating. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and expect it to sucker over time, forming a productive hedgerow if not controlled. It tolerates extreme cold and drought once established, making it a reliable choice where other fruiting shrubs struggle.
sources: Comparative agronomic performance of saskatoon cultivars, Canadian Journal of Plant Science

planting.note: Plant in spring with ample room; Parkhill grows into a large, wide shrub and blooms about a week later than most saskatoons, which can help dodge late frosts.

directions: Parkhill is a U.S.-origin saskatoon cultivar that has been widely adopted in Canadian commercial plantings for its large, deep blue, tangy-sweet fruit borne in long, heavy clusters. Its later bloom time reduces frost damage to flowers compared with earlier-blooming cultivars, improving fruit set reliability in variable spring weather. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil and give it plenty of space, since mature plants can reach 15 feet tall and wide. Harvest in clusters once berries turn deep blue and detach easily, similar to picking blueberries.
sources: Gardening at USask, University of Saskatchewan
